query: For reported HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure, what testable hypothesis could enable Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior to be predicted more rapidly and accurately under tensile and fracture testing than with established simulations? State the hypothesized rationale, the measurable gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency, circumstances in which the hypothesis may fail, relevant supporting evidence, and a predeclared result from independent measurements that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A physics-informed machine learning surrogate model that integrates microstructural descriptors of the hierarchical heterostructure can predict the Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior of as‐fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 more rapidly and with improved accuracy compared to conventional simulations.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 high‐entropy alloy with a conventional, hierarchically organized microstructure.
generation.intervention: Development and application of a neural network surrogate model that embeds continuum mechanics constraints and is trained on multi‐modal datasets (combining simulation outputs and independent experimental measurements) capturing the microstructural features of the hierarchical heterostructure.
generation.conditions: Under tensile testing regimes covering elastic, plastic, and fracture behaviors, as well as standardized fracture tests that replicate conditions used in independent experimental measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: Key microstructural descriptors such as grain size, phase distribution, and compositional heterogeneities inherent to the hierarchical architecture.
generation.mechanism: By embedding physical constraints into the ML model’s architecture, the surrogate model learns the mapping from detailed microstructural descriptors to mechanical responses. This integration allows the model to bypass computationally intensive full-scale simulations while accounting for the heterostructural influences on elastic and plastic behavior as well as fracture initiation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model is expected to yield prediction errors (e.g., RMSE) that are lower by approximately 10% relative to established simulation methods, and to reduce computational time by at least an order of magnitude.
generation.baseline: Conventional simulation approaches (e.g., continuum mechanics models or atomistic simulations) that are either too computationally demanding or insufficiently accurate in capturing the complex hierarchical microstructure.
generation.boundary: The model’s predictive performance may degrade if the microstructural characteristics fall outside the range of those represented in the training data—for example, under processing conditions that induce unexpected phase distributions or when extreme loading and environmental conditions are applied which were not included during training.
generation.uncertainty: While preliminary evidence supports the feasibility of integrating physics-informed constraints into ML models for HEAs, uncertainties remain regarding the model’s transferability to all potential microstructural variabilities and extreme testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Develop the proposed physics-informed neural network surrogate model using combined simulation data and independent experimental measurements of microstructural descriptors from HfNbTiVAl10 samples. Then, conduct tensile and fracture tests to independently measure Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior. Compare the ML predictions with both experiments and conventional simulation outputs.
measurements: Young’s modulus from elastic region stress-strain data
Yield strength determined from 0.2% offset method
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the surrogate model's prediction error is not significantly lower (i.e., fails to achieve an ~10% improvement in RMSE) compared to established simulation methods, or if the computational time is not reduced by at least an order of magnitude, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Accurate machine learning models for predicting the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) require a comprehensive dataset compiled from various established databases [,,]. Our study focused on both single-phase BCC HEAs and BCC+B2 HEA composites to capture a broad spectrum of mechanical behaviors and phase interactions, thus enhancing the robustness and generalizability of our predictive models. We prioritized compression data over tensile data due to their greater availability and consistency, specifically targeting yield strength σYS and plasticity εf. Tensile properties were excluded as they involve different mechanisms and are less frequently reported for BCC phases.

AbstractThe aim of this work was to provide a guidance to the prediction and design of high-entropy alloys with good performance. New promising compositions of refractory high-entropy alloys with the desired phase composition and mechanical properties (yield strength) have been predicted using a combination of machine learning, phenomenological rules and CALPHAD modeling. The yield strength prediction in a wide range of temperatures (20–800 °C) was made using a surrogate model based on a support-vector machine algorithm. The yield strength at 20 °C and 600 °C was predicted quite precisely (the average prediction error was 11% and 13.5%, respectively) with a decrease in the precision to slightly higher than 20% at 800 °C. An Al13Cr12Nb20Ti20V35 alloy with an excellent combination of ductility and yield strength at 20 °C (16.6% and 1295 MPa, respectively) and at 800 °C (more 50% and 898 MPa, respectively) was produced based on the prediction.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, machine learning, prediction, strength, structure

There are 370 RCCAs data points from the DFT calculation. A total of 90% of data were utilized for training, and 10% were used to test and validate the results. The three ML models used in this work are random forest (RF) regressor, gradient boosting regressor (GBR), and XGBoost (XGB) through the Scikit-learn library [], which is also used for data preparation and model assessment. The RF model is an ensemble approach consisting of many decision trees to improve prediction accuracy and reduce overfitting by averaging the trees. The samples of the training dataset may reappear in the single tree due to sampling replacement, also known as bootstrapping. GBR and XGB are multi-purpose machine learning methods that can handle both classification and regression problems. The GBR is a type of ensemble model having an iterative collection of tree models, and it is capable of learning from the previous model’s mistakes. The XGBoost [] is a powerful machine learning method that makes a quick decision by implementing boosted decision trees efficiently and effectively.
